description: The built-in data types of MATLAB (numeric classes, logical, char, string, cell and struct), the functions that create and convert between them, and the array-creation, sizing and reshaping functions that every other part of the language builds on. Everything in MATLAB is an array, so these functions apply uniformly from scalars to N-D arrays.

tools.name: double
tools.description: Converts its input to the double-precision floating-point class, which is MATLAB's default numeric type. Use it to promote integers, logicals, chars or single values before arithmetic that needs full precision, and to turn a char array into its Unicode code points. Numeric literals typed at the command line are already double, so explicit conversion is only needed when data arrives as another class.
tools.usage: Y = double(X)

parameters.name: X
parameters.description: Numeric, logical, char or string-convertible input array.

tools.notes: Integer arithmetic in MATLAB saturates rather than wrapping, and mixing two different integer classes is an error, so converting to double first is a common fix. `isfloat` and `isa(x,'double')` test the class.

tools.name: single
tools.description: Converts an array to single-precision (32-bit) floating point, halving memory use at the cost of roughly 7 significant decimal digits instead of 16. Use it for large data sets where memory dominates, or to match the precision of GPU kernels and embedded targets. Arithmetic between a single and a double produces a single result.
tools.usage: Y = single(X)

parameters.name: X
parameters.description: Numeric, logical or char array to convert.

tools.example:
x = single(pi)
whos x
eps('single')
tools.notes: Accumulating long sums in single can lose accuracy; `sum(x,'double')` accumulates in double while keeping the input single.

tools.name: int32
tools.description: Converts an array to the signed 32-bit integer class, rounding to the nearest integer and saturating at the class limits instead of overflowing. The sibling functions int8, int16 and int64 behave identically with different widths. Use integer classes for index-like data, image pixel values, bit manipulation and interfaces with C code.
tools.usage: Y = int32(X)

parameters.name: X
parameters.description: Numeric, logical or char array to convert and round.

tools.notes: int32(2.5) returns 3 because MATLAB rounds halves away from zero. Combining int32 with int16 raises an error; convert one operand explicitly. Use `idivide` for integer division with a chosen rounding rule.

tools.name: uint8
tools.description: Converts an array to the unsigned 8-bit integer class, with values clamped to the range 0 to 255. This is the native class of most images read by `imread` and of raw byte buffers, so it appears constantly in image and file I/O code. uint16, uint32 and uint64 are the wider unsigned equivalents.
tools.usage: Y = uint8(X)

parameters.name: X
parameters.description: Numeric, logical or char array; values are rounded then saturated to [0,255].

tools.notes: Scaling a uint8 image usually requires `double(img)/255` first, otherwise the division truncates to integers. `imshow` expects uint8 in [0,255] or double in [0,1].

tools.name: intmax
tools.description: Returns the largest value representable by a given integer class, as a value of that class. Use it to test for saturation, to build sentinel values, or to document the valid range of an integer variable. Called with no argument it reports the maximum for int32.
tools.usage:
v = intmax
v = intmax(classname)

parameters.name: classname
parameters.description: Integer class name such as 'int8', 'uint16', 'int64'.

tools.example:
intmax('uint8')
intmax('int64')
x = int16(32760) + int16(100)   % saturates at intmax('int16')
tools.notes: The companion `intmin(classname)` returns the smallest representable value (0 for unsigned classes); note that negating it saturates, so -intmin('int8') is 127. For floating-point limits use `realmax`, `realmin`, `eps` and `flintmax`.

tools.name: logical
tools.description: Converts a numeric array to the logical class, mapping zero to false and every nonzero value to true. Logical arrays are what relational operators return and what MATLAB requires for logical (mask) indexing. Use it when a numeric 0/1 array must be used as a mask, or to make intent explicit.
tools.usage: L = logical(A)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Numeric array; must not contain NaN, which raises an error.

tools.notes: Indexing with a double 0/1 array is interpreted as positional indexing and usually errors on index 0, which is why explicit `logical` conversion matters. `islogical` tests the class; `true` and `false` create logical arrays directly.

tools.name: char
tools.description: Creates a character array, converting numeric code points to characters or concatenating multiple inputs into a padded character matrix. Character arrays are the classic MATLAB text type, written with single quotes, and each element is one 16-bit character. Use `char` when interfacing with older APIs or code that expects char rather than the newer string class.
tools.usage:
C = char(A)
C = char(A1, A2, ..., An)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Numeric code points, a string array, a cell array of character vectors, or several inputs to stack as rows.

tools.example:
char(72, 101)
C = char('abc', 'defg')
size(C)
double('a')
tools.notes: Stacking inputs pads shorter rows with trailing spaces, which is why char matrices are awkward for ragged text; prefer `string` or a cell array of character vectors. `cellstr` converts a padded char matrix back to a cell array with the padding removed.

tools.name: string
tools.description: Creates a string array, the modern MATLAB text type in which each element holds a whole piece of text of any length. Written with double quotes, string arrays support element-wise text functions, comparison with ==, and missing values via `<missing>`. Use `string` to convert numbers, char arrays, cellstr or categorical data into string arrays.
tools.usage:
str = string(A)
str = "text"

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Numeric, char, cellstr, categorical, datetime or duration input to convert.

tools.example:
s = string([1 2 3])
names = ["alpha"; "beta"];
names == "beta"
strlength(names)
tools.notes: `"abc"` is a 1-by-1 string, while `'abc'` is a 1-by-3 char array; `strlength` gives text length for strings, `numel` gives 1. Use `ismissing` to detect missing string elements.

tools.name: cell
tools.description: Preallocates a cell array of empty matrices, the container type that holds values of different classes and sizes in each element. Index with parentheses to get a sub-cell-array and with braces to get the contents. Use cell arrays for ragged data, lists of file names, or collections of heterogeneous results.
tools.usage:
C = cell(n)
C = cell(sz1, ..., szN)
C = cell(size(A))

parameters.name: sz1,...,szN
parameters.description: Dimensions of the cell array to create.

tools.notes: Growing a cell array in a loop without preallocation is slow. `cellfun`, `cell2mat` and `num2cell` are the main companions; `iscell` tests the class.

tools.name: struct
tools.description: Creates a structure array whose elements have named fields holding arbitrary values. Passing a cell array as a field value creates a struct array with one element per cell, which is the idiomatic way to build record lists. Structures are the standard way to bundle related values and to return multiple named results from a function.
tools.usage:
s = struct(field1, value1, ..., fieldN, valueN)
s = struct()

parameters.name: fieldN
parameters.description: Field name as a character vector or string.

parameters.name: valueN
parameters.description: Field value; a cell array creates a struct array with one element per cell.

tools.notes: `struct('a', {})` creates a 0-by-0 struct array with field a. Use dynamic field names `s.(fname)` to access a field whose name is held in a variable.

tools.name: class
tools.description: Returns the name of the class of a variable as a character vector, for example 'double', 'string', 'cell' or a user-defined class name. Use it for diagnostics, for dispatching on type, and in error messages. For a yes/no test prefer `isa`, which also accounts for inheritance and class categories.
tools.usage: cname = class(obj)

parameters.name: obj
parameters.description: Any MATLAB value.

tools.notes: `class` returns the exact class only; a subclass of double-derived types will report its own name, so `isa(x,'numeric')` is usually the better test.

tools.name: isa
tools.description: Tests whether a value is of a given class, of a subclass of it, or of a broad category such as 'numeric', 'float' or 'integer'. Use it in argument validation and in code that must behave differently for different input types. It returns a logical scalar, so it drops straight into `if` statements and `assert`.
tools.usage:
tf = isa(obj, ClassName)
tf = isa(obj, classCategory)

parameters.name: ClassName
parameters.description: Class name to test against, for example 'double' or 'MyClass'.

parameters.name: classCategory
parameters.description: One of 'numeric', 'float' or 'integer'.

tools.example:
isa(int8(1), 'integer')
isa(single(1), 'float')
isa(1, 'numeric')
isa(containers.Map, 'handle')
tools.notes: Related predicates include `isnumeric`, `ischar`, `isstring`, `iscell`, `isstruct`, `islogical` and `isobject`. In an `arguments` block, class names are validated automatically.

tools.name: cast
tools.description: Converts a value to a class named at run time, or to the class of another variable. Use it when the target type is data-driven, for instance when writing generic code that must return results in the same class as its input. Values are rounded and saturated exactly as the equivalent direct conversion function would do.
tools.usage:
B = cast(A, newclass)
B = cast(A, 'like', p)

parameters.name: newclass
parameters.description: Target class name as a character vector or string.

parameters.name: 'like', p
parameters.description: Cast to the class and complexity of prototype p (also preserves gpuArray-ness).

tools.notes: `cast(...,'like',p)` is the recommended pattern for code that must also run on GPU or in generated C code. Use `typecast` instead when you want to reinterpret the underlying bits without converting the value.

tools.name: typecast
tools.description: Reinterprets the raw bits of an array as a different data type without changing the underlying bytes. Use it for binary protocol work, reading packed file formats, or inspecting the IEEE representation of floating-point numbers. The total number of bytes is preserved, so the output length changes when the type width changes.
tools.usage: Y = typecast(X, type)

parameters.name: X
parameters.description: Full, non-complex numeric or char array to reinterpret.

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: Target class name such as 'uint8', 'single', 'int32', 'double'.

tools.example:
b = typecast(single(1), 'uint8')
typecast(b, 'single')
dec2bin(typecast(single(-1), 'uint32'), 32)
tools.notes: Results depend on the machine byte order; use `swapbytes` to switch endianness. typecast does not accept complex, sparse or logical input.

tools.name: zeros
tools.description: Creates an array of zeros of a given size and class, the standard way to preallocate before a loop. Without arguments it returns the scalar 0; with one argument it returns a square matrix. Preallocating with zeros avoids the repeated reallocation that makes growing arrays in loops slow.
tools.usage:
X = zeros(n)
X = zeros(sz1, ..., szN)
X = zeros(___, classname)
X = zeros(___, 'like', p)

parameters.name: sz1,...,szN
parameters.description: Size of each dimension.

parameters.name: classname
parameters.description: Output class, for example 'int32', 'single', 'uint8'.

parameters.name: 'like', p
parameters.description: Match the class, sparsity and complexity of prototype p.

tools.notes: `zeros(2,3,'like',gpuArray(1))` creates the array directly on the GPU. Use `ones`, `nan`, `inf`, `true` and `false` for the corresponding fill values.

tools.name: ones
tools.description: Creates an array filled with the value 1, with the same size and class options as `zeros`. Use it to preallocate, to build constant matrices by scaling (`5*ones(3)`), or to construct design matrices with an intercept column. It accepts a class name or a 'like' prototype.
tools.usage:
X = ones(n)
X = ones(sz1, ..., szN)
X = ones(___, classname)

parameters.name: sz1,...,szN
parameters.description: Size of each dimension.

parameters.name: classname
parameters.description: Output class name.

tools.notes: For a constant other than 1, `repmat(c, m, n)` or `c*ones(m,n)` both work; repmat avoids a multiply and preserves non-numeric fill values.

tools.name: eye
tools.description: Creates an identity matrix, or a rectangular matrix with ones on the main diagonal and zeros elsewhere. Use it as a starting point for linear algebra, to build permutation and selection matrices, or to represent an initial state transition. `eye(n,'like',A)` matches the class and sparsity of an existing matrix.
tools.usage:
I = eye(n)
I = eye(n, m)
I = eye(___, classname)

parameters.name: n, m
parameters.description: Number of rows and columns; a single argument gives a square matrix.

parameters.name: classname
parameters.description: Output class name.

tools.example:
I = eye(3)
A = magic(3);
norm(A * inv(A) - eye(3))
speye(4)
tools.notes: For large identity matrices use `speye` to avoid storing the zeros. `eye` with a 'like' prototype preserves sparsity and GPU residency.

tools.name: rand
tools.description: Generates uniformly distributed pseudorandom numbers in the open interval (0,1). Use it for Monte Carlo sampling, random test data and randomized algorithms; scale and shift the output to reach any other interval. The sequence is controlled by the global random number stream, which `rng` seeds for reproducibility.
tools.usage:
X = rand(n)
X = rand(sz1, ..., szN)
X = rand(___, classname)

parameters.name: sz1,...,szN
parameters.description: Size of the output array.

parameters.name: classname
parameters.description: 'double' (default) or 'single'.

tools.notes: Always call `rng(seed)` before random generation you need to reproduce; `rng('default')` restores the factory Mersenne Twister state. `randn` gives normal deviates and `randi` gives integers.

tools.name: randn
tools.description: Generates pseudorandom numbers from the standard normal distribution (mean 0, standard deviation 1). Scale and shift with `mu + sigma*randn(...)` to sample any normal distribution. It is the workhorse for simulating measurement noise and for stochastic simulations.
tools.usage:
X = randn(n)
X = randn(sz1, ..., szN)
X = randn(___, classname)

parameters.name: sz1,...,szN
parameters.description: Size of the output array.

parameters.name: classname
parameters.description: 'double' (default) or 'single'.

tools.notes: randn shares the same random stream as `rand` and `randi`, so seeding with `rng` controls all three.

tools.name: randi
tools.description: Generates uniformly distributed pseudorandom integers in a specified range. Pass a scalar imax for the range 1:imax or a two-element vector [imin imax] for an arbitrary range. Use it for random indices, bootstrap resampling, dice-roll style simulations and random integer test data.
tools.usage:
X = randi(imax)
X = randi(imax, sz1, ..., szN)
X = randi([imin imax], ___)
X = randi(___, classname)

parameters.name: imax
parameters.description: Upper bound of the range 1:imax.

parameters.name: [imin imax]
parameters.description: Explicit inclusive range.

parameters.name: classname
parameters.description: Integer or float class for the output.

tools.notes: For sampling without replacement use `randperm` instead. `randi` returns double by default even though the values are integers.

tools.name: true
tools.description: Returns logical 1, or an array of logical ones of a given size. Use it to preallocate logical masks and to create an all-pass filter that later code narrows down. The companion `false` creates logical zeros with the same syntax.
tools.usage:
T = true
T = true(n)
T = true(sz1, ..., szN)

parameters.name: sz1,...,szN
parameters.description: Size of the logical array to create.

tools.notes: Logical arrays use 1 byte per element, so masks over large data are cheap. `true(n)` allocates an n-by-n array, not a scalar.

tools.name: linspace
tools.description: Generates a row vector of linearly spaced points between two endpoints, inclusive of both. Unlike the colon operator you specify the number of points rather than the step, which guarantees the last value is exactly the endpoint. Use it for plotting grids, sampling a function over an interval and building time vectors.
tools.usage:
y = linspace(x1, x2)
y = linspace(x1, x2, n)

parameters.name: x1, x2
parameters.description: First and last values of the vector.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Number of points (default 100).

tools.notes: linspace(a,b,1) returns b, not a. For a fixed step use `a:step:b`, which may stop short of b when the step does not divide the interval evenly.

tools.name: logspace
tools.description: Generates a row vector of logarithmically spaced points between 10^a and 10^b. Use it for frequency axes in Bode plots, for sweeping parameters across orders of magnitude, and for log-log plot grids. The default output has 50 points.
tools.usage:
y = logspace(a, b)
y = logspace(a, b, n)

parameters.name: a, b
parameters.description: Exponents; the vector runs from 10^a to 10^b.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Number of points (default 50).

tools.notes: Pass `pi` as the second argument to end the vector exactly at pi rather than 10^pi, a documented special case.

tools.name: colon
tools.description: The range operator, written `a:b` or `a:step:b`, which creates a regularly spaced vector; `colon(a,b)` is the functional form. Used on its own inside an index, a bare colon means 'all elements along this dimension'. It is the most common way to build loop ranges and to slice arrays.
tools.usage:
x = a:b
x = a:step:b
x = colon(a, step, b)
A(:, k)   % all rows of column k

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Start value.

parameters.name: step
parameters.description: Increment; may be negative. Default 1.

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: Limit; the last element does not exceed it.

tools.notes: Floating-point steps accumulate rounding error, so `0:0.1:1` may not end exactly at 1; use `linspace` when the endpoint matters. `A(:)` reshapes any array into a column vector in column-major order.

tools.name: numel
tools.description: Returns the total number of elements in an array, equal to the product of its dimensions. Use it whenever you need a count rather than a shape, for example to size a preallocation or to loop over every element. For a string scalar it returns 1, because the whole text is a single element.
tools.usage: n = numel(A)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Any array, cell array, struct array, table or object.

tools.example:
A = magic(4);
numel(A)
numel({1, 'two', [3 4 5]})
numel("hello")
tools.notes: `length` returns the largest dimension, not the element count; `numel` is almost always the safer choice for loops. Use `strlength` for the number of characters in a string.

tools.name: size
tools.description: Returns the dimensions of an array, either as a row vector, as separate outputs, or for a single named dimension. Use it to validate input shapes, to loop over rows or columns, and to build arrays that match an existing one. Since R2019b you can request several dimensions at once with a vector of dimension numbers.
tools.usage:
sz = size(A)
szdim = size(A, dim)
[m, n] = size(A)
[sz1, sz2] = size(A, [1 2])

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: Dimension number, or a vector of dimension numbers.

tools.notes: With two output arguments on an N-D array the trailing dimensions are folded into the last output, so `[m,n] = size(rand(2,3,4))` gives n = 12. `height`, `width` and `ndims` are clearer for specific needs.

tools.name: length
tools.description: Returns the length of the largest dimension of an array, and 0 for an empty array. It is convenient for vectors, where it is the number of elements. For matrices it can be misleading, so prefer `numel`, `size` or `height` in general code.
tools.usage: L = length(X)

parameters.name: X
parameters.description: Any array.

tools.example:
length(1:7)
length(zeros(3, 9))
length([])
tools.notes: length(A) is equivalent to max(size(A)) for non-empty A. For tables use `height`; for text use `strlength`.

tools.name: ndims
tools.description: Returns the number of array dimensions, which is always at least 2 in MATLAB because scalars and vectors are stored as 2-D arrays. Use it to branch between matrix and N-D array code paths and to validate that an input has the expected rank. Trailing singleton dimensions are not counted.
tools.usage: n = ndims(A)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Any array.

tools.example:
ndims(5)
ndims(rand(2, 3))
ndims(rand(2, 3, 4))
ndims(rand(2, 3, 1))
tools.notes: ndims(A) equals numel(size(A)). Use `ismatrix`, `isvector`, `isscalar` and `isrow` for more specific shape tests.

tools.name: isempty
tools.description: Returns true when an array has zero elements, that is when at least one dimension is 0. Use it to guard against operating on empty results, for example after `find` or a filtering operation that matched nothing. It works for numeric arrays, strings, cells, structs and tables alike.
tools.usage: tf = isempty(A)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Any array or container.

tools.notes: An empty string scalar `""` is not empty by this test (it has one element); use `strlength(s)==0` instead. `isempty` is not the same as all-zero.

tools.name: reshape
tools.description: Changes the dimensions of an array without changing its data or element order, which MATLAB stores column first. The product of the new dimensions must equal the original element count, and one dimension may be given as [] for MATLAB to infer. Use it to turn vectors into matrices, to flatten data, and to split an interleaved stream into channels.
tools.usage:
B = reshape(A, sz1, ..., szN)
B = reshape(A, sz)
B = reshape(A, [], n)

parameters.name: sz1,...,szN
parameters.description: New dimension sizes; at most one may be [].

parameters.name: sz
parameters.description: Row vector of new dimensions.

tools.example:
v = 1:6;
reshape(v, 2, 3)
reshape(v, 3, [])
reshape(v, 2, 3)'
tools.notes: Because filling is column-major, `reshape(1:6,2,3)` puts 1 and 2 in the first column. To fill row-wise, reshape transposed dimensions and then transpose the result.

tools.name: repmat
tools.description: Tiles a copy of an array in a grid to build a larger array. Use it to expand a row or column to matrix size for element-wise operations, to preallocate struct or cell arrays, and to construct block patterns. With scalar input it is a fast way to build a constant array of any class.
tools.usage:
B = repmat(A, n)
B = repmat(A, r1, ..., rN)
B = repmat(A, sz)

parameters.name: r1,...,rN
parameters.description: Number of copies along each dimension.

tools.notes: For arithmetic, implicit expansion usually makes repmat unnecessary and faster: `A - mean(A)` broadcasts automatically since R2016b. repmat remains the right tool for preallocating struct and cell arrays.

tools.name: cat
tools.description: Concatenates arrays along a specified dimension: 1 for vertical, 2 for horizontal, 3 and higher to stack into pages. Use it when the concatenation dimension is computed at run time, or to build 3-D stacks of images or matrices. All inputs must agree in every dimension except the one being joined.
tools.usage: C = cat(dim, A1, A2, ..., An)

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: Dimension along which to concatenate.

parameters.name: A1,...,An
parameters.description: Arrays to join; sizes must match in all other dimensions.

tools.notes: cat(1,...) is [A; B] and cat(2,...) is [A, B]. Use `cat` with `deal` or comma-separated lists to join all elements of a cell array: `cat(1, C{:})`.

tools.name: squeeze
tools.description: Removes dimensions of length 1 from an array, turning for example a 1-by-1-by-5 array into a 5-by-1 vector. Use it after indexing a single page or slice out of an N-D array, when the result would otherwise keep awkward singleton dimensions. It never operates on 2-D arrays, so row and column vectors are left alone.
tools.usage: B = squeeze(A)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Array with one or more singleton dimensions.

tools.notes: squeeze leaves 2-D arrays unchanged, so a 1-by-5 row vector stays a row vector. Use `reshape` when you need an exact target shape.

tools.name: permute
tools.description: Rearranges the dimensions of an N-D array according to a permutation vector, generalizing the transpose to any number of dimensions. Use it to reorder image data between height-width-channel conventions, to move a batch dimension, or to prepare data for functions that operate along the first dimension. `ipermute` applies the inverse rearrangement.
tools.usage: B = permute(A, dimorder)

parameters.name: dimorder
parameters.description: Vector that is a permutation of 1:ndims(A) giving the new dimension order.

tools.notes: For 2-D arrays `permute(A,[2 1])` is the same as `A.'` (non-conjugate transpose). `pagetranspose` transposes each page of an N-D array in one call.

tools.name: circshift
tools.description: Shifts array elements circularly, wrapping values that fall off one end back to the other. Use it for cyclic buffers, for aligning signals, and for neighbour differences on periodic data. Specify a positive shift to move elements toward higher indices and a negative one for the other direction.
tools.usage:
Y = circshift(A, K)
Y = circshift(A, K, dim)

parameters.name: K
parameters.description: Number of positions to shift; may be a vector to shift several dimensions.

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: Dimension to shift along.

tools.example:
circshift(1:5, 2)
circshift(1:5, -1)
A = magic(3);
circshift(A, 1, 2)
tools.notes: Unlike `shiftdim`, which moves dimensions, circshift moves data. For non-wrapping shifts, index with a padded array or use `lagmatrix`-style manual indexing.

tools.name: flip
tools.description: Reverses the order of elements along a dimension, defaulting to the first non-singleton dimension. Use it to reverse a time series, to flip an image vertically or horizontally, or to convert between ascending and descending data. `flipud` and `fliplr` are the fixed-dimension shortcuts for matrices.
tools.usage:
B = flip(A)
B = flip(A, dim)

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: Dimension along which to reverse (1 = rows, 2 = columns).

tools.example:
flip([1 2 3 4])
A = magic(3);
flip(A, 1)
flipud(A)
fliplr(A)
tools.notes: flip works on strings, cell arrays and tables as well as numeric data. For a matrix, `flip(A)` reverses rows because dimension 1 is the first non-singleton dimension.

tools.name: sort
tools.description: Sorts array elements in ascending or descending order, column by column for a matrix, and optionally returns the permutation indices. Use the second output to apply the same reordering to related arrays. It handles numeric, logical, char, string, datetime, duration and categorical data.
tools.usage:
B = sort(A)
B = sort(A, dim)
B = sort(___, direction)
[B, I] = sort(___)

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: Dimension to sort along.

parameters.name: direction
parameters.description: 'ascend' (default) or 'descend'.

parameters.name: 'ComparisonMethod'
parameters.description: 'auto', 'real' or 'abs' for complex input.

parameters.name: 'MissingPlacement'
parameters.description: 'auto', 'first' or 'last' for NaN and missing values.

tools.notes: NaN values sort to the end by default. Use `sortrows` to sort a matrix or table by chosen columns while keeping rows together, and `issorted` to test without sorting.

tools.name: unique
tools.description: Returns the distinct values of an array in sorted order, with optional index outputs that map between the original and unique arrays. Use it to deduplicate data, to build a lookup of category labels, and together with `histcounts`-style counting to tabulate occurrences. The 'rows' option treats whole rows as single items.
tools.usage:
C = unique(A)
C = unique(A, 'rows')
[C, ia, ic] = unique(___)
C = unique(___, 'stable')

parameters.name: 'rows'
parameters.description: Treat each row of a matrix or table as a single entity.

parameters.name: 'stable'
parameters.description: Keep the original order of first appearance instead of sorting.

parameters.name: 'first'/'last'
parameters.description: Which occurrence index to return in ia.

tools.example:
[C, ia, ic] = unique([3 1 3 2 1])
counts = accumarray(ic(:), 1)
unique(["b" "a" "b"], 'stable')
tools.notes: The third output ic reconstructs the original with `C(ic)`, making it ideal for grouping. For grouping in tables prefer `findgroups`/`groupsummary`.

tools.name: find
tools.description: Returns the linear indices of nonzero (or true) elements, optionally limited to the first or last n matches, and optionally as row/column subscripts. Use it to locate elements that satisfy a condition and to convert a logical mask into positions. For plain selection, logical indexing is faster and clearer than find.
tools.usage:
k = find(X)
k = find(X, n)
k = find(X, n, direction)
[row, col] = find(___)
[row, col, v] = find(___)

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Return at most n indices.

parameters.name: direction
parameters.description: 'first' (default) or 'last'.

tools.notes: `v(v>4)` is preferable to `v(find(v>4))`. find returns an empty array when nothing matches, so always check with `isempty` before indexing the result.

tools.name: accumarray
tools.description: Accumulates values into bins defined by subscripts, applying a function (sum by default) to all values mapped to the same output element. It is the vectorized way to compute group sums, counts, means and maxima without a loop. Combine it with the third output of `unique` or with `findgroups` to aggregate by category.
tools.usage:
A = accumarray(subs, val)
A = accumarray(subs, val, sz, fun, fillval)

parameters.name: subs
parameters.description: Column vector or matrix of positive integer subscripts.

parameters.name: val
parameters.description: Values to accumulate; scalar values are expanded.

parameters.name: sz
parameters.description: Size of the output array, or [] to infer.

parameters.name: fun
parameters.description: Function handle applied to each group, for example @max or @mean.

parameters.name: fillval
parameters.description: Value for output elements with no contributions.

tools.notes: Non-sum functions are applied per group and must return a scalar. For table data, `groupsummary` and `splitapply` are more readable alternatives.
